title: Stratification by CVD risk equations does not inform the use of aspirin for primary prevention in older adults

sections.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Aims</jats:title> <jats:p>We aimed to determine whether commonly recommended cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk equations would inform a risk–benefit discussion on the role for aspirin as a primary prevention strategy for CVD in older persons. We assessed aspirin’s effect on CVD and major haemorrhage on the basis of baseline levels of CVD risk using risk scores pertaining to the older age groups.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Methods and results</jats:title> <jats:p>We used (i) the Framingham risk score (FRS), (ii) the atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), and (iii) the European SCORE2-OP equations to calculate 10-year predicted CVD risk. Participants were classified into predicted risk tertiles (T): lower (T1), intermediate (T2), and higher (T3) risk. We identified CVD and major haemorrhagic events utilizing each risk equation’s definition of CVD. The CVD event rate increased from T1 to T3 using all risk equations. For participants with the greatest CVD risk (T3) according to FRS and ASCVD, aspirin vs. placebo was associated with a proportional 28% (95% CI: 54–95%) and 25% (95% CI: 57–97%) reduction in CVD risk, respectively. However, there was no significant effect of aspirin for individuals with low (T1) or moderate (T2) risk nor according to the SCORE2-OP tertiles. Rates of major haemorrhagic events were the highest in all T3 groups. Aspirin was associated with a significant increase in bleeding events vs. placebo in all T1 groups and FRS and SCORE2-OP T2 groups. The reduction in CVD events in FRS and ASCVD T3 groups was offset by a 32% and 15% increased risk of bleeding, respectively.</jats:p> </jats:sec> <jats:sec> <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title> <jats:p>In older persons with no prior cardiovascular events, current CVD risk scores do not identify any subgroups with overall net clinical benefit from low dose aspirin.</jats:p> </jats:sec>
